t: Minimum Operations to Make the Array K-Increasing — LIS Over Residue Classes
o: **Understanding the problem.** The k-increasing condition links an element only to the one k positions earlier, so the array splits into k independent chains: indices i, i+k, i+2k, ... for each residue i in [0, k). For `[4,1,5,2,6,2]` with k = 2 the chains [4,5,6] and [1,2,2] are already non-decreasing — 0 operations; with k = 3 the chains are [4,2], [1,6], [5,2], of which two violate the rule — 2 operations. An operation rewrites any element into any positive integer, so the cheapest repair keeps a longest non-decreasing subsequence (LNDS) of each chain untouched and rewrites everything else: cost = chain length − LNDS. Summing over chains gives the answer. Since n reaches $10^5$, the quadratic LIS DP is too slow at full load, motivating the patience-sorting variant.
k: arr[i-k] <= arr[i] couples only same-residue indices — solve k independent non-decreasing problems.
Changed values are unconstrained positives, so keeping the LNDS and rewriting the rest is always optimal: ops = length - LNDS.
Non-decreasing allows duplicates, so the binary search must be upper_bound / bisect_right, not lower_bound.
Chains partition the array, so total work stays O(n log n).

a.n: Approach 1: Quadratic DP LIS per Chain
a.i: The classic O(L^2) longest non-decreasing subsequence DP applied to each extracted chain: dp[i] = 1 + max(dp[j]) over earlier j with seq[j] <= seq[i]. Perfectly transparent, fine for small inputs, but the sum of squared chain lengths reaches ~10^10 when n = 10^5 and k = 1.
s: Extract chain i: arr[i], arr[i+k], arr[i+2k], ...
Run the O(L^2) non-decreasing LIS DP on the chain.
Add len(chain) - lis(chain) to the answer.
Repeat for residues 0..k-1 and return the total.
a.t: Quadratic in chain length (sum of L_i^2) — too slow at n = 10^5 with k = 1.
a.sp: O(L) — the dp array of one chain.

a.n: Approach 2: Patience Sorting With Binary Search (Optimal)
a.i: Maintain tails[], where tails[t] is the smallest possible tail of a non-decreasing subsequence of length t+1. Each x lands at bisect_right(tails, x) — upper_bound because equal values may extend the same subsequence. The chain's cost is its length minus |tails|; sum across the k chains.
s: Start tails = [] for the current chain.
For each x: pos = upper_bound(tails, x).
Append x if pos == len(tails), else overwrite tails[pos] = x.
After the chain, add len(chain) - len(tails) to the answer.
a.t: O(n log n) — n elements total, each costing one binary search.
a.sp: O(L) — the tails buffer of the longest chain (up to n).

w: Voice the decomposition out loud ("residue classes are independent") — that observation IS the problem. Pitfalls: using lower_bound (strict-LIS) so duplicates like [2,2] count as violations; treating the whole array as one sequence instead of k chains; mis-extracting chains (start at residue i, step k). Follow-ups: make the array strictly k-increasing (switch to strict LIS with lower_bound), or cap the number of allowed edits and ask for feasibility.
